Lecture Notes on the Purification of the Six Sense Organs: A Record of a Dream (Preface) The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra, Part Three: The Announcement for the Ritual Fasting Period (*jiǎizhāi*) [The following is the main body of the text: **Record of a Dream** On the night of the twenty-third day of the second month of the year Wuchen (1628), during the ritual fasting period for the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), I dreamed that I was traveling through the Southern Mountains. I beheld a magnificent temple, its gates and courtyards vast and imposing. Within, there were monks and laypeople gathered in great numbers, all clad in bright, pure robes. They were engaged in chanting and recitation with deep reverence. I entered the hall and saw the Venerable Master [Zhiyi] seated upon the high seat. His countenance was serene and majestic, his voice resonant as he expounded the Dharma. He was elucidating the meaning of the "Purification of the Six Sense Organs" (*liugen qingjing*). As he spoke, light emanated from his mouth, illuminating the entire assembly. At that time, I felt a profound sense of clarity and purity. My six senses were suddenly purified, and I perceived all phenomena as being like empty space—unobstructed and ungraspable. I then realized that the so-called "six organs" are originally the Buddha-nature; their defilement arises from deluded attachment, while their purification comes from the awakening to reality. The Master further explained that the "purification of the six organs" is not merely a matter of external discipline, but the manifestation of the inherent purity of the mind-ground. When the eye-organ is purified, one perceives the true nature of all forms; when the ear-organ is purified, one hears the Dharma-sound of the Buddhas; when the nose-organ is purified, one smells the fragrance of liberation; when the tongue-organ is purified, one tastes the flavor of the Dharma-treasure; when the body-organ is purified, one experiences the touch of the Tathagata’s power; and when the mind-organ is purified, one realizes the wisdom of the ultimate truth. As the lecture drew to a close, the Master placed his hand upon my head and said, "If you can maintain this purity in every thought, you shall attain the stage of non-retrogression. Upon waking, I felt my heart filled with joy and a renewed resolve to cultivate the path. This record is intended to serve as a reminder to those who practice the Way, encouraging them to seek the purification of their six organs and to realize the original enlightenment of the Lotus Sutra. [End of Preface] **Lecture Notes on the Purification of the Six Sense Organs** [The main body of the lecture follows... **The Meaning of the Title** The title "Purification of the Six Sense Organs" refers to the restoration of the six faculties to their original, unobscured state. In the mundane world, these six organs are clouded by ignorance and attachment, leading to suffering and delusion. In the supramundane realm, they are transformed into the six "liberations" (*liujie*), becoming gateways to the Buddha-way. The *Lotus Sutra* states: "The six organs are pure, and the three karmas are likewise pure. This signifies that when the practitioner attains the stage of non-retrogression, their six organs become identical to the Buddha's organs, capable of manifesting various transformations to save sentient beings. Therefore, the cultivation of the purification of the six organs is the core practice of the *Lotus Sutra*. It is not an external ritual but an internal realization of the true nature of the mind. By contemplating the emptiness and non-arising of all phenomena, one severs the roots of delusion and returns to the source of purity. [The lecture continues with detailed exegesis on the specific practices and doctrinal points of the purification of each organ. **Conclusion** In summary, the purification of the six organs is the ultimate goal of the Mahayana path. It requires the practitioner to integrate the teachings of the sutras with daily practice, maintaining mindfulness and wisdom in all activities. Only through such diligent cultivation can one truly embody the spirit of the *Lotus Sutra* and achieve the great vow of universal salvation. [End of Lecture Notes] [The following is the announcement for the ritual fasting period: **Announcement for the Ritual Fasting Period** The third volume of the *Fahua xuanyi* has now been completed. We hereby announce the commencement of the ritual fasting period for the purpose of deepening our understanding and practice of this profound teaching. All practitioners are requested to observe the precepts, abstain from worldly distractions, and dedicate themselves to silent meditation and scriptural study. May the merit of this assembly bring peace to the nation and benefit to all sentient beings. [End of Announcement] [End of Volume Three]

A Record of Plums by the Si River:
Regarding those plums whose sights and sounds have been known to the world—those in Wu are at Xuanmu, the private estate where the Grand Commandant Deng Xuan wandered and dwelt;
those in Hangzhou are at Gushan, the hermitage where the Eminent Scholar Lin Buo took his meals and lived with his wife. Both...

It has long been recorded in local chronicles and transmitted among both the refined and the common folk. Yet, why is it that the plum trees of my own hometown, Sishui, are scarcely mentioned at all in such records?
Is it not because they lie so far from the prefectural seat, tucked away in remote mountain villages, making them inconvenient for sightseeing;
thus, even the Mountain Historian failed to collect and compile accounts of them, much like how Mount Tiantai was not included among the Five Sacred Peaks?
Is this not what is meant by being omitted from the standard records? The Si River lies thirty *li* southwest of the administrative seat of Wuxing Prefecture, at the northern foot of Mount Jing.
Over a hundred or so *mu* of land alongside the mountain are planted entirely with plum trees;

because the local inhabitants rely on the plums as their source of livelihood, they do not prune them excessively nor intermingle them with other species. When the warmth of spring begins to blossom forth, I occasionally return there.

I went out from the village to observe it. Concentrating my spirit for a single glance, the embroidered colors seemed to dazzle the heavens. Holding tea, I sat long in meditation; brocade carpets followed the ground.
Fragrant souls wafted about, and I constantly feared that Mount Luofu would enter my dreams and cause the flower-petals to fall.

Gradually, my thoughts drifted to the brows of Lady Shouyang, where the patterns were interlaced and overlapping, their origins and exits lost in mystery. Pausing and sighing in admiration, I was so captivated by the desire for beauty that I forgot to return. And northward...
Facing the Si-guan stream, it occasionally floats upon clear, shallow brooks; to the south, it is backed by green mountains, further manifesting the brilliance of ice and frost.

Yet its profound and distant charm, its vast and expansive vistas, are such that they cannot be fully grasped by the mind and eye at any single moment, nor can they be exhaustively described by pen or tongue;
only those of expansive spirit may realize them for themselves. In short, even Gu-shan and Xuan-mu pale in comparison.

This is to bow downwind. Yet, I am moved by a profound reflection. When the plum blossoms of Mount Gushan and Xuanmu open, the men and women of Suzhou and Hangzhou—traveling in teams of four horses and on horseback—come and go in endless succession, flocking to view them and spreading their praises far and wide.
Even women and children know that there are plum trees in the two places [of the Five Mountains], yet in my own hometown by the Si River, none have heard of them.
Aside from a solitary mountain woodcutter or two, those who are obsessed with the land rarely recognize their fragrance;
among them, there was but one person who sighed in appreciation. As I was lingering there, reciting and pondering over them, everyone pointed at me and laughed, saying, "This man is a fool!"
"Now the branches have not yet borne fruit; why do you all cling so devotedly to these empty flowers? I smiled and asked, "Do you not find joy in this?

"Is it that Heaven is more parsimonious toward that place than this? He then laughed with a sense of sudden clarity and said, "These are both merely objects.
Why would Heaven be more parsimonious toward those and alone lavish its bounty upon these?

Indeed, although the plum trees in both locations are appreciated by people, as for those at Xuanmu, their extraordinary branches and elegant trunks are likely to be plucked and broken by visitors eighteen or nineteen times out of twenty; the remainder are merely ordinary."
The branches are bare and the trunk remains alone; at Mount Gu, the stinking winds swirl in confusion, and the fragrant souls have been slaughtered until nothing remains.

Yet my plum tree by the Si River stands serene and unharmed. Is it not because that which nurtures itself in obscurity endures long, while that which displays its brilliance like dew is easily crushed?
I have heard that on the southern bank of the Si River, this was once the residence of a prominent official during the late Song dynasty. Now...

This was because not only was his realization of the Way brilliant and refined, but it was also vast and expansive.
He is one who possesses the complete talent required to respond to the world. Ten years have passed since I last went to see him, and his cultivation has grown even more firm.

All those of the clergy and laity from the four quarters, as well as the discerning ones of my own village, all look toward the Master’s emergence, hoping he will spread the moisture of a universal cloud so that plants, trees, insects, and even the smallest creatures may all realize their Buddha-nature; yet the Master remains serene and has no intention of leaving.

His realization of the Way was brilliant and clear, and for a long time he has been revered by the monastics throughout the land. Furthermore, he possessed the steadfastness of one who nurtures the Way and the talent to respond to the world.
For nearly twenty years, both the clergy and the laity have looked up to him with earnest anticipation for his transformative guidance, yet he has not emerged. Is it perhaps because he...?

Preface to the Essential Meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

The essential meaning of the *Vajracchedikā* is profound and perfect, and its spiritual manifestations are remarkably evident. Consequently, those who have provided commentaries and promoted its circulation number no fewer than several hundred families.

Although the chrysanthemum and the orchid each excel in their own way, when one examines their origins and conclusions, they are found to follow one another in succession; for every ten works, eight or nine are identical.

I have examined and contemplated this repeatedly; it seems to be the Buddha’s own words, yet it remains somewhat cumbersome and its internal logic lacks sufficient coherence. Whenever I approached its exposition and instruction, I could never reach full clarity.
Only recently, while reading the great *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures, did I discover their essential intent. Applying that understanding to this sutra, it fits together like two halves of a tally.
Relying upon the wisdom-observation of true emptiness, I have washed away minor doubts and realized that all eighty-one sections are Mahāyāna;
this is the purport of the Prajñāpāramitā division. I have accordingly marked them out according to the text, so that the meaning is ample and the wording contains no superfluous characters;
it is as if "black dragon pearls" are nestled together. Only the phrasing is somewhat direct and entirely lacks literary ornamentation, yet the underlying principles are clear and lucid.

Regarding the sections (*sthāna*), they are not explicitly listed in the main chapters. As for the profound and hidden points of the fundamental tenets, even a single character is explained in detail;
this is precisely because one wishes for both the refined and the common to understand them together, so that the meaning of the sutra may be easily clarified.

As for the topical headings (*kośa*) prefixed to the text, the purpose lies in ensuring that every word and phrase has its proper place and that the internal logic (*sira-pattra*) flows through from beginning to end, so that the "flowers" of the teaching do not remain scattered and directionless, nor does the Buddha’s speech become stagnant, redundant, or cumbersome.
It is merely a matter of removing these entanglements. How could I dare say that this interpretation differs from that of the former sages?

Eating grain amidst these surroundings, one may likewise turn the Wheel of Dharma, thereby responding from above to the donor’s heart.

Observing with reverence the green dancers at their slender waists within the palace, one awaits the new sprouts before the camp of the slender willows; as red blossoms fly across the brocade screens, one feeds fine steeds amidst the groves of great trees.
As I write this, my hands tremble with fear; I am overwhelmed by a sense of dread and anxiety.
[End of] *Suiyuan Jizha* (Miscellaneous Writings Collected According to Circumstances), Part One; *Suiyuan Jizha*, Part Two.
Written by Lingyao of Quanzhang at Lengyan Jangsi Temple in Jiahe,
in collaboration with the two monastic communities of Hucheng and Jizhao at Mount Shuangjing, for the purpose of editing and carving the Tripitaka:
Lingyao, Dharma Master of Lengyan Temple, respectfully addresses this letter to the various assemblies of the two cloisters of Hucheng and Jizhao on Mount Shuangjing.

Under the seat of the Zen Master, I, Yu, have heard that the gentleman applies himself to the root. Now, the great Tripitaka in its volumes is actually shared by both the Lêng-yen and Shang-shan monasteries.
Since this is the fundamental matter and a priority for urgent tasks, I venture to inform you with this letter.
Although the ancients carved the canon for the universal benefit of all within and beyond the seas, the printing blocks were stored at Hua-ch’êng Chih-chao for circulation.

Within the quarters of Lengyan Jangsi Temple, we have set aside the surplus proceeds for the carving of the Tripitaka. Externally, this shall serve to adorn the Triple Gem and nurture the worthy and sagely;

there will be no need to crawl at the doors of donors or struggle for the sake of religious affairs. Furthermore, from the remnants of the boards used for the mountain-top printing blocks, we shall produce additional printing blocks.

It is sufficient to provide for several mouths at a time, allowing one to settle the mind and advance on the Path. There is no need to seek alms from a thousand households or to rely on worldly conditions through such entanglements.

To establish three halls is to solidify the foundation; the intention behind this is profoundly deep. Yet, as no practice endures forever, dilapidation will eventually arise within the scriptural quarters.

They know only to covet the surplus, yet do not know how to organize the precious Dharma-treasures on the mountain; they know only the surface of the woodblocks, yet do not know how to repair and carve the blocks for the Tripitaka.
As the years and months pass, the wood becomes infested with insects and decays; the great canon of the future may well await its transformation into dust.

Based solely on the records of the request for the canon by the unwise Yúan-ān in the year Bingchen, three people read it together and found that the volumes and fascicles were out of order and disordered.
Omissions and errors are so numerous they cannot be enumerated; there are countless instances where ten, a hundred, five, six, or even one or two characters have been lost.
This spring, when Master Danguī requested the Tripitaka, he found that the initial volumes of the sutras and śāstras were frequently incomplete.

Master Huanglong examined them and discovered that the missing characters were particularly numerous. Inferring the cause, it was because the printing blocks were not made of iron or stone, and having endured for many years—

That [the woodblocks] have become decayed and worm-eaten is but the natural course of things. Recently, the assembly of Dharma-protectors from Songling sent a letter to me, their humble servant, expressing deep concern that if the printing blocks for the canon are not repaired, the Buddha-dharma will be obstructed;

they feared that the compassionate life-blood of the two Great Masters, Baizhang and Zongmi, would soon be cast away like a single current flowing eastward. Therefore, they entrusted me with the task of repairing the engraved blocks and reorganizing the Great Canon.

I, Bu-hui, have reverently read this and am filled with shame, having no place to hide. For I was utterly ignorant of the meritorious virtues of our fundamental patriarchs of the Three Monasteries, as if I had never even heard their names.
Yet, a layman alone has been so earnest toward the Dharma-gate, so sincerely attentive to its concerns.
How great is the disparity between his wisdom and my own, and between his worthiness and my unworthiness! It is truly cause for shame. This is solely because of the Great... [text truncated]

Whether within or without the borders of the Qing Empire, this is the only edition of this collection. Those who have come from afar to request it have not declined the hardships of thousands of miles and many years of travel.

Yet, once they arrive at our monastery and open the scrolls for inspection, they find them blurred, erroneous, and missing even a single character, making the meaning difficult to discern—how much more so when such errors abound! If one wishes to come to the temple to correct these omissions, then the journey...
The road to Liaodong is vast and distant; mountains and rivers obstruct and deepen the way.

If one wishes to seek verification from others, yet cannot raise the bleached bones of Kāśyapa to question them, then one must know that when even a single character on a wooden tablet is damaged and left unrepaired, it signifies that not a single drop of the Tathāgata’s lifeblood has reached the four seas of the world.
How great is this transgression! This is truly a matter worthy of serious discourse.
They substitute scriptures, pointing to a deer as a horse, seeking only to complete their sets and volumes so they may trade them for gold and money.
They do not realize that by obstructing the Dharma and deceiving the monks, their crime merits banishment to the realm of clay figures.

Even if the craftsmanship is somewhat coarse, when tigers and rhinoceroses escape their cases or tortoises and jade are shattered from their boxes, whose fault is it? As for the abbot, he says nothing but "there is too much fire-food."
It is merely a matter of small amounts. The monastic quarters concern themselves only with whether there is a surplus of provisions;

the mountain retreats concern themselves only with whether the "board-head" (the communal rice ration) is sufficient or not. Yet they do not realize from where this surplus for fire-food and these board-head rations actually come.
Is it not the case that they all originate from the fundamental source of the *zangban* (storage granary)? Now, the *zangban* is being abolished and no longer maintained.
Yet you look back to weigh and measure the gain of a mere *zhi* or *chu*. Is it not that you have abandoned what is great and distant to calculate what is small and near?
Or is it that, like one stealing gold at high noon, you see only the profit and fail to consider the fundamental?
Though it is said that the heroic man pursues fame while the common person pursues profit, by your conduct, even as for profit, I fear you will not succeed.
It can be preserved for a long time. Why is this? If one does not repair it now, twelve parts will decay and become worm-eaten;

if one does not repair it after five years, fifteen boards will break; and if one does not repair it after ten years, the entire set of printing blocks for the Tripitaka will sit there like mummified corpses.
Now, if there is a foundation, one may seek profit; but if one examines the foundation and finds none, how can profit be obtained? Thus it is said: [The text continues with: "All..."
The Master may attain great enlightenment through this; yet the masters of the three halls will surely all say, "I am concerned only with the thickness of my daily profit;
what does the decay and infestation of the printing blocks in future years have to do with me?"

Therefore, everyone sits by idly and fails to intervene. I fear that once the Dharma-protectors of Zhuili, Danyang, Jinxi, and Wujiang all rise together to manage these "tadpole-era" affairs, they will be so preoccupied with spitting out their indignation that they will surely have no leisure to sit peacefully and swallow the Great Canon.
Even if the Great Dharma-protector does not see the monk's faults now, before the Judge Yama’s desk in a future life—
"Who would dare swallow iron balls and molten copper on their behalf? We who have left the household life—how could we fail to believe in cause and effect?

The elder Dharma-protector Zhou Anshi of Wujiang said: "If one does not repair the printing blocks for the Tripitaka but seeks only to fatten the household and enrich oneself, the protective deities will repeatedly descend to issue warnings and will no longer grant their protection. All of these...

This is something Your Excellency has witnessed and personally experienced; how can you not stand in awe? I have privately traced the events over the past few years and find that the printing blocks could not be repaired, for there was a specific reason.
Since the outbreak of hostilities in the Jia-yin year, the mountain passes have been blocked and no one has come to request the Tripitaka.

Consequently, the scriptures within the monastery have almost entirely vanished, and all hope for the printing blocks on the mountain has been lost. Even the several members of the monastic community currently residing here...
How could I, with my meager resources, take from what remains after filling my own empty belly to repair the damage caused by moth-eaten fragments?

However, in the past, when I was not yet wise and examined the Tripitaka, whenever I encountered missing pages or omitted characters in the forest retreats that rendered the meaning and principles difficult to comprehend, I never failed to stamp my feet, stare wide-eyed, and lament and curse those who were responsible for its preservation.
Having long eaten the public's salt without performing my duties, I have now personally come to occupy this position.
Abbot: How could I further endure the bitter insults of the people of the world and even those of my own circle?
For this reason, the carving of the Great Canon has been my long-standing aspiration; it is the urgent priority for establishing the fundamental source.
How much more so, then, when I am exhorted by the assembly of Dharma protectors? Upon inquiry, I learned that over six hundred leaves of the entire set of woodblocks were slightly damaged by insects.

The carving will involve several hundred thousand characters, including the costs for boiling the woodblocks and other related expenses; the total expenditure will not exceed one thousand *qian*, and the project will not take more than three years to complete.
Compared to the time when the various patrons first proposed this undertaking, it would have required no more than the funds for a single volume.
Having been entrusted by the assembly of donors, I, though lacking wisdom, have consented to oversee the completion of this work. However, all of you gentlemen are disciples of Master Mi.
The descendant [Miao Yi] says: I am further fortunate that we have been able to exert our strength together with one mind to assist in this noble undertaking.
Some have managed the carving and engraving, while others have traveled afar to solicit support. These are those whom I look up to and earnestly entreat.

As for the few remaining wooden blocks, beyond what is required for labor costs, there is still a lack of funds; I, being of little wisdom, shall offer my robes and sell my alms-bowl to raise the necessary funds.

I dare not let this involve the various gentlemen. My intention lies solely in re-editing the entire Tripitaka so that the Dharma-treasure may circulate widely, ensuring that the compassionate life-blood of the two patriarchs, Bodhidharma and Amoghavajra, does not flow away like water, and that the meritorious deeds of the donors who sponsored the carving do not become mere wood shavings.
This is my sole aspiration. Second, it is to ensure the eternal preservation of the *Sūtra of the Adamantine City* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which are shared treasures.

This is fundamental, and it must not be treated with laxity. Now, when the Old Fool moved the mountains or the Great Giver drained the sea, people surely laughed at them as fools and considered their capacity to be small.
Yet, when sincerity reaches its ultimate limit, perhaps even devas and nāgas will provide secret assistance so that success is achieved;
this cannot be known for certain. My words may seem tedious, but I hope you will not hold me in fault.
Again, an Epistle Requesting the Repair of the Tripitaka Woodblocks on Behalf of the Dharma Protectors of Wujiang (with the accompanying letter attached).
I respectfully venerate the honorable elders, the Great Dharma Protectors. Your talent surpasses that of the court of Ye; your literary brilliance illuminates the celestial court.
In establishing merit and virtue, you have already brought radiance to the two realms; in both teaching and Chan, you have spread the single thread of the Way throughout all things. It is only...

The legacy of this paradigm remains in the land of China for a thousand autumns and ten thousand years. That you, Venerable Sir, look up to my lofty style with such reverence is something I have long desired, not merely for a morning or an evening.

Lately, due to the initial establishment of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* assembly, I was personally unable to attend upon you in person. Suddenly, you have bestowed upon me these precious words, an honor that exceeds all bounds.

To be unworthily favored by such magnificent robes is a source of profound shame; that I have consequently allowed myself to speak rashly is a transgression from which I can find no escape. Because of this—

The printing blocks of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) were decaying and infested with woodworms, on the verge of collapse. Thereupon, I, the unworthy Yao, was commanded to repair and re-carve them, employing every means to propagate and protect them.

I am deeply aware that the earnest and profound instructions entrusted to me at Mount Lingjiu were most diligent; thus, seeing those of like mind, I rejoice. When Zibo visited me, I was living in seclusion in a mountain village.

Having once encountered the scriptures as if they were characters eaten by insects, I gazed upon the canonical texts and felt sorrow that long-standing worms had encroached upon the sacred words. *Jun* (the signature).
I received the command to bring [this matter] forth; it seems to accord with my long-held aspiration. I shall serve the public and depart, not declining wherever I may be assigned.

However, I reflect that while the person is humble, the task is grand, and it is difficult to initiate; moreover, considering the passage of months and years, how could it be easily brought to a successful conclusion?

For this reason, though my heart leaps with joy, my steps falter and hesitate. I look up in reliance upon you, Great Person, to share your light and bestow your illumination, extending your hand and eye so as to enable [the undertaking].
I, the unworthy Yao, have gathered what was omitted and supplemented what was deficient, gradually restoring the jade case.

It is my hope that the Great Treasury of the Buddha’s Jewels may be reestablished throughout the four seas, so that the vast merit of this act of patronage and protection may be clearly manifest for all eternity. As I write these words, I am overcome with a sense of profound gratitude and trepidation.
I reflect deeply: Your Reverence’s understanding and practice both transcend the ordinary; wisdom and compassion are exercised in tandem.
You have mastered the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma without exception, and you have integrated the schools of Dharma-characteristics and Chan into a non-dual harmony.

For long have all quarters admired your reputation, and in this age of the Final Dharma, our reliance upon you is especially profound. We, the unwise, remain hidden away in Songling and have not yet had the opportunity to pay you a personal visit.
In this chamber for the tally-sticks, gazing afar at the compassionate model, my longing for reliance and refuge is but keen.

Herein I open the Fangce Canon (the "Case-Repository" Canon), which was established through the great vow of the Venerable Zibo to create this superior condition. Initially carved at Mount Wutai, it was subsequently dedicated to Mount Shuangjing;
both Jizhao Monastery and Huacheng Monastery served as the locations where the blocks were engraved and stored. This was the arrangement made by our predecessors.

A sound regulation was established: as soon as printing occurred, repairs were to follow to prevent decay and insect damage. The costs for such repairs were to be covered by the proceeds from the sale of the wooden blocks.
Unintentionally, over time, the Dharma became obscured; later generations treated the established laws with contempt, vying with one another to seize control and arbitrarily destroy them.

Although the sutras were still being printed, the damage and erosion gradually increased. Day by day they declined and month by month they diminished—how could this ever come to an end? And yet, new...

As for the old printing blocks, it is unknown what has become of them; their surrender and destruction would indeed be appropriate. It is truly a matter of great joy that the gentlemen of your esteemed province have made a pact for a thorough investigation and clearance.
This is truly a grand undertaking for the eradication of demons and the removal of abuses. I am deeply gratified that your Reverence has halted your journey to reside at Lêng-yen Monastery.

It is here that the registers of the Earth Treasury (Ti-tsang) were disseminated; as the woodblocks had fallen into disrepair, this provides an opportunity to fulfill my responsibility to restore them.

I humbly entreat the Venerable Master to radiate great brilliance and extend his broad and long tongue, so that the "lion-insects" may not come to devour the flesh, and the Dharma-treasure may forever attain its majestic dignity.
Not only will those of dull wit like myself dance with hearts full of devotion, but even within the Venerable One’s eternal *dharmakāya* light, you shall surely open your countenance and smile.
As for the noble friend Wang Jinqing, he is well-suited to the task of carving the Tripitaka.
Having recently received the entrustment of various donors, I have resided in the mountains for many years. I am most fortunate to have gained extensive experience and proficiency;

yet, upon detailed inquiry, it appears there is much to be discussed and deliberated. In hastily drafting this letter to my fellow practitioners of the Dharma, I have not had the opportunity to sign it.
I hope you will all graciously examine it with compassion. Respectfully submitted by Zhou Bangbin, Wu Zhiji, and others.

Preface for the Carving of the Tripitaka Woodblocks by Great Master Zibo and Fellow Donors and Protectors: The Sanskrit manuscripts have been translated into the Chinese fascicle format, and the scriptures together with their commentaries have been compiled into a single canon (*pitaka*) to facilitate its circulation.
This ensures that those who sit in discussion may have access to it within their own homes and read it individually. [This project has already] reached its third ascent...

As for the nine superior qualities: it can be carried on one's back while walking swiftly; even the families of scholar-officials may store it alongside their books and rank it among the "Two You" (the two mountains of the Kunlun range).
One may freely fish and harvest from it to profoundly investigate the original source; no merit is greater than this.

However, being merely wood-carved, it lacks the durability of metal or stone and suffers the affliction of decay and insect damage over time. If this is lost and not repaired, in the future—[it will become like] a feather...
How deeply lamentable this transformation! For the Northern Canon has been melted down for coinage, and the Southern Canon is incomplete and lacks corroboration.

Thus, these volumes of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are not only a fundamental auspicious treasure for the Great Qing Empire, but are truly the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom for all within and beyond the four seas.
It is heard that the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gazes toward Jambudvīpa three times each day.
I prostrate in homage. Because this contains the written Prajñāpāramitā, the wisdom-life of devas and humans, as well as the bodhi of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, all depend upon it.

If even a single character of the printing blocks here were not maintained, then not a single point of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and wisdom-life would circulate among heaven and earth; how much more so when they are being diminished daily and ruined monthly?
In the end, all things return to non-existence. I, lacking wisdom, have by chance been appointed as the abbot; I wish to honorably restore and maintain [this tradition].

Examining the transmission of the Buddha-dharma to the East, from the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty to the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, the translated sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, along with the commentaries composed by various worthies, total five thousand and forty-eight fascicles.
Together they constitute the authentic record of one complete canon (*piṭaka*). From the Kaiyuan era...
On the day of Gengwu, during the final years of Emperor Wen of the Zhide era, more than four thousand nine hundred scrolls were translated and composed in succession.
Combined with the existing records from the Kaiyuan and Chongfu periods, these formed a collection of ten thousand scrolls of sacred texts.

Subsequently, the translations produced during the fragmented Tang, the Five Dynasties, the Song, and the Yuan, as well as the commentaries, exegeses, and recorded sayings of the Ming dynasty, far exceeded those of the preceding eras. If one were to consider the situation at that time...
The cost of carving this original edition is not even a hair on a horse’s body or a grain of millet in a great granary compared to the expenses required for its repair today.
Thus, the investment is small while the entire Great Canon is preserved; the effort expended is slight while the achievement attained is magnificent.
I dare not keep this to myself, but venture to inform my fellow practitioners. Furthermore, I have heard that in the past, I shared the same resolve with the Great Master Zibo.
When the Tripitaka was first carved, there were the various masters He Danyang of Jinxī, Yu Songling, Zhou Jiahe, Lu Fengzhu, and Bao, who,

while manifesting in the bodies of secular officials, fulfilled the vows of Bodhisattvas and brought the project to completion. Thus, as I, one of little wisdom, now undertake the restoration of the Tripitaka,
I must likewise look forward to the offerings of the subsequent incarnations of these masters to provide their assistance.
This is for the sake of principle.
Furthermore, the Chief Administrator Jinghui respectfully submits this memorial:

The site of enlightenment first began as a place where offerings were made in accordance with the source; now, throughout the monasteries of the successive sages, the great gate has been opened wide, and its importance is particularly emphasized.

With a universal mind, he served as the administrator for three years; with one shout, he clarified the fundamental principle. Seeking conditions across a thousand chambers, he entered the wondrous through the four truths.
I respectfully address the Great Virtue, the esteemed Master [Name]: your roots are firm and steadfast, like the *nán*, *zǐ*, and *yùzhāng* trees; yet you possess the gentle beauty of conduct.

Rare indeed are those free from blemish. Like a *gui* or *zhang* jade vessel, or the bright moon, his essence is perfectly refined. Having fully realized the vast capacity of the Elder Chan, the waters and clouds have returned to virtue.
His integrity and steadfastness are like that of Shengjiang Han; the dragon-elephants revere his influence. He recommends the thick to others while dwelling in the thin;

when a friend seeks warmth from him, he feels it as if warming himself. When he restrains himself for the sake of others, even if the multitude are thereby satiated, he conducts himself as if he himself were the one being satisfied.

Although it is said that this is brought about by the power of his vows, it is essentially both innate and effortless. He governs all things with humility and harmony, such that his reputation spreads among both the ordained and the laity.
His sincerity arises from the core of his being, and his spiritual renown overflows beyond the borders of every province.

One might say he is without shame before those on the first and second stages (*bhūmi*), while he possesses ample leisure compared to those on the third and fourth fruits (*phala*). In recent times, he has followed in the footsteps of Śāriputra, suddenly reviving a long-standing model.
The Hu monk Guangxi, relying upon his own karmic retribution, occupied a specially adorned seat of fearlessness within the inner court.

He earnestly entrusted the transmission of the *Udumbara* scriptures to beginners who delight in solitude; he did not seek to rival the merit of Buddhas and patriarchs, but truly desired that his grace extend to humans and devas.

This is surely because they have galloped alongside the divine illumination to transcend the long-lasting [delusions], and raced side-by-side with perfect clarity to eliminate their dullness and ignorance.

As for me, I am but a tiny herb by a medicinal fence, a scorched sprout in the garden of awakening. My cultivation of contemplation is faint and subtle; I have not yet stepped across the threshold of the Four Reliances.

The propagation of the Dharma is laborious and halting; it is difficult for me to even glimpse the walls of the Fifth Stage. It is therefore fitting that I nurture my simplicity in this desolate wilderness and continue my long journey.

How could I have expected this? Last autumn, as we walked arm-in-arm, you already granted me your heart’s accord; this New Year, as we floated our cups together, you ultimately entrusted me with the mission.

In the past, Layman Lu was submerged in obscurity at Xiaiban, fully intending that he would remain unheard of for all eternity; yet when Chan Master Yin urged him to open the hall, it became a magnificent event for a thousand years.
Now I, [Name], have suddenly been graced by such an encounter, feeling a profound sense of gratitude for being allowed to share in this light. I fear I may fail to live up to your lofty expectations.

My feelings of trepidation are as great as bearing up Mount Tai; therefore, I have looked up to follow the precedent of declining an office twice or thrice, yet I have again been burdened by the arrival of the first and second summons.
I still rely upon Your Majesty’s great virtue of *dāna* (generosity) to harmonize the urgent and the slow, so that the Precious Vehicle may gallop straight upon the broad highway.

I have therefore commissioned this unworthy one to open up both the ultimate and the conventional truths. Grasping the singular mystery, I shall cause all phenomena to vanish into universal stillness, so that this single gate may be free from the peril of structural collapse, while all the myriad plants may bathe in the moisture of the universal cloud.
I await only the harmonious chirping of birds seeking companions, looking up to respond to the consolation of those with like voices.
As new blossoms rain down upon the seat, may we share equally in the intimate reliance of the Many-Jeweled Stūpa. At this writing, I am without words.
I submit this most sincere petition for your protection.
Furthermore, I respectfully address the Honorable Protectors of the Dharma of Pure Wisdom.
To the esteemed elders and great patrons, the disciples of the Master: May the lakes and mountains nurture your refined excellence, and may the precious ocean expand your causal realization.
The Honored One vies in brilliance; manifesting his body according to those to be saved, he utterly forgets his noble status when descending, yet honors and glory are employed to rescue all beings.
It is by his office that the rice-juice flows through irrigation canals and divine trees rain down food. Thus, fragrance streams from every pore and vessels are filled with precious broth.

How could this merely be to lead the two other schools [Brahmanism and Taoism] to their preeminence? Indeed, he is loftily adorned with the One Vehicle to guide all across. As for me, I contemplate his monastery...

Yan Honghuo, whose fundamental vocation was the protection of the Dharma, gradually ascended to the Lingzhi Hall of Haiyuan and the Dao-li Palace. There, his reception was suddenly renewed as he was entrusted with the Pure Wisdom of the Lotus School.

His golden voice resonated lightly, and jade gifts were bestowed from afar. This was surely intended to reveal the unique excellence of Vulture Peak so that all who suckle at their mothers' breasts might record it;

furthermore, it served to fully expound the sole perfection of the Buddha’s teachings on the Dragon Slope, equally opening the muddled consciousnesses of all. Alas! Such a magnificent undertaking rivals the era of King Śreṇika.

Your peerless greatness is vast indeed; your far-reaching legacy surpasses that of the Sui monarchs, whom none can equal. As for me, I am but one of small roots and small shoots, fit only for humble dwelling at the foot of the forest.
Moreover, in such a great state and a magnificent monastery, I fear it would be difficult for me to sit peacefully within the cloud-hall.

Therefore, in receiving this command, I feel a profound anxiety as if treading upon thin ice or standing over a deep abyss. Reflecting upon myself, I am filled with much trepidation, yet I still dare to present my head like a rat or my horns like a ram, looking up toward you.

Relying on the great donor, who has consistently provided extensive protection and suppressed bandits, he has been diligent in restraining the unvirtuous. Furthermore, he has removed our branding and restored our noses;
thus, I, though lacking wisdom, have attained inner and outer tranquility by following the ancestral injunctions to manifest them for the world.

May this endeavor begin its commencement and reach its conclusion; then, as for the distribution of funds and the allocation of provisions, one realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) through non-delusion. Thus it was heard.

The Dharma has been transmitted through the scriptures; I have approached the Jewel Mountain without retreating. Reverently following the arrival of the mysterious bird, I long to dwell at the lofty gate and gaze upon the elder’s lush red peaches.
Having entered the chamber of the Master to behold the celestial being, I am overwhelmed with a sense of profound emotion and awe as I take up this brush.
Furthermore, we, the patrons of Eikyū-in, submit this petition:

When the Northern Dipper spreads its light, the sovereign at the throne obtains the aid of the *gui* and *long*; when the teachings of the Western Heaven are propagated, the city of *khandhaka* relies upon the worthiness of the Wangs and Xies.

When the enlightened ruler and his virtuous ministers rejoice together, their songs reach the *qingyun* clouds; may we likewise be protected so that these teachings may circulate, and pray that we may uphold the golden instructions.

The fortunes of this nation rely upon you for their longevity; the destiny of the Dharma depends upon you for its prosperity and stability. We respectfully venerate the venerable elders, the great protectors of the Dharma.

Like麒麟 (qílín) and 鳳凰 (fènghuáng) at the head of the court, you provide the foundation for auspiciousness through your counsel; like the morning stars above the heavens, you are looked up to for your diligent brilliance.

You sleep in tranquility while draped in brocade, declining honors that would otherwise befit the eight-petaled flowered tiles; yet when the embers are lit and the grass is inspected, your five-colored brush adds luster to the imperial edicts.

A Divine Plan: Its great voice resounds with solemnity; surely it rests with those wearing the *zhài* (deer-antler) cap. Moreover, while the multitude may halt their progress, the true path truly returns to the chestnut steed.
Are there not the worthies of Gao Yao, Kui, Shen, and Fu? All alike bear the heavy responsibility of being the sovereign's throat, tongue, thighs, and arms.

Yet, as for the literary man’s enlightened vocation, he shall not forget the testament of the Golden River; manifesting his total essence and great function, he shall once again follow the division of the Vulture Peak.
Thus, he was able to establish his achievements, his virtue, and his words, accomplishing the magnificent enterprise of the "Three Immortalities.

Whether through teaching, dhyāna, or vinaya, he elucidated the Great Matter; he surpassed Yang and Li in his mastery of the Spring and Autumn Annals, and excelled Su and Wang in the depth of his realization.
Lamenting that the Dharma-gate had fallen into corruption and that the seeds of wisdom were being swept away, he [established] the Yongshou Monastery.

A phantom array of four flowers has been spread; the seats are now prepared. This unworthy one, [I], strives to propagate the "Single Rain" (the universal teaching). Opening the seal upon the jade-like pearls within the cinnabar case, they soar like rosy clouds and fly like drifting mists.
As the contents of the baskets and boxes are presented at this banquet, I prostrate myself to receive this imperial gift. May its abundance dispel the darkness and its moisture nourish the rivers.

Yet, reflecting upon my own meager learning, I am but half a leopard—my wisdom incomplete and my capacity insufficient. While comparing the three tracks of the Way, I still fall short of the eloquence of the Sage; as I look toward the great carriage, I realize my journey is but a small portion of the whole.
