In vain we recount the rhythmic beats of the *húqié* melody; how tragic! The lotus flowers at the tips of the trees, the autumn winds across the marshes—Zhou Lang pays them no heed.
The dressing mirror stands empty; the silk fan has been cast aside. Red leaves fall, yet their message cannot be conveyed. Like Empress Chen in the Changmen Palace, or Lady Mei in the Xigong.

My sorrowful feelings for those parted are stirred at the southern ford; I wipe away my tear-filled eyes by the eastern wall. Sparse raindrops scatter like the soul of the Goddess of the River not returning;
glistening dewdrops fall like the endless weeping of the Consort of Xiang. Alas! Her voice has fallen into the yellow dust, and neither carriage nor horse knows her place.
Some gather lotus flowers, others gather lotus seeds, yet the elegance of her grace has suddenly vanished. I say: in years past...
I encountered her to the south of Nanhu Lake. Her makeup was exquisite and her movements graceful; she moved with the slow, languid gait of a lotus.
Now that I have come, the three ponds are already falling into decay. If even things are thus, how can a person endure it? Consequently, I lingered there, unable to bear to depart.
It was because of weariness that he required the company of those close to him. Sometimes they would converse with him under the morning breeze and the waning moon;

sometimes they would comfort him amidst the evening rain and the morning mist. As for the flowers, they seemed to frown and smile, as if bidding him farewell or welcoming him back, appearing just as they had when he was alive.
We are truly fellow travelers, fallen from our home and meeting here at the ends of the earth; why need we have known one another before?
Between us lingers a lingering trace of fragrance that silently permeates the senses. Your coquettish charms still evoke the former airs of a courtesan’s quarters;
your aged allure is like the frown of Xi Zi, yet your gestures grow ever more seductive. I addressed her with a stern countenance, saying: "I am a student of the Way."
O person! This mind has already become like a flower-cotton soaked in mud; it no longer follows the eastern wind to flutter wildly up and down.
You employ your own methods, which, within my Dharma, are as far apart as the wind and the cattle. From now on, cease this; do not disturb my mind.
However, you possess excellent qualities, yet you were born at an unfavorable time and planted in an unsuitable place; therefore, you have suffered the humiliation of exhaustion and brokenness.
Yet you do not yet know this? Now, West Lake is a world of honor and disgrace, a sanctuary for wine and meat.
When Zhuangzi contemplated the transformations of nature, the transformations reached him; when you dwell amidst honor and disgrace, disgrace reaches you—this is the inevitable course of principle.

Why did you not realize this sooner? Had you first understood that cultivated beauty is but a delusion and awakened to the depravity of the multitude’s hearts, then what need would there have been for [all this]?

Only when things have fallen into decay will one finally realize their emptiness. From this day forward, why not each conceal our brilliance and sever all traces, bidding a long farewell to the world of men?

Washing away the dross of vanity, let us hide away among the streams and mountains; thus, perhaps, honor and disgrace shall no longer concern our inner being, and by knowing the rarefied, we may preserve our own natural integrity.
Today is the eighteenth year since the year Wumu (1898). On the full moon of the sixth month, I, with a single...
I boarded a skiff to seek out the lotus of my former days, but its traces had vanished into the distance. I beheld only a single expanse of lake-light and the indigo hue of a thousand mountains;

the moon was bright and white, delighting the people, while the wind was gentle and lingering, stirring all things. Unconsciously, my gaze grew weary as if seeking the void, yet my vexed breast was suddenly cleansed.
My body and world seemed to have perished, and the dust-laden mind of the mortal self naturally extinguished itself. As the Elder Su Dongpo said: "Vast and boundless..."
It is as if one were leaning upon the void or riding the wind, with no knowledge of where one rests;

it is as if one has transcended the world and stands alone, shedding the wings of mortality to ascend as an immortal—this is what is most urgent here. In a mere moment, the shifting golden waves turn unstable;
in an instant, one lies within the deep mirror of the lapis lazuli wall. Above and below are vast and indistinct, yet there appears only the single wheel of the heart-moon, faintly visible.
The echoes raise doubts as to whether they are those of Su Xiaoxiao; yet she does not forget the sorrowful weeds. At Qingling, her girdle-bells circle in vain as she returns to the moon;
her soul seems to hear a faint sound, as if Prince Wenxuan were still chanting: "The setting clouds and solitary wild ducks fly together; the autumn waters and the vast sky are one color.
Yet there are no lotuses at the temple in the heart of the lake, nor are there any at the Shrine of Master Xuan. On the sands of Gushan, the ripples rise.
There were no lotuses. Indeed, when Xi Yuejing departed, Wang Qing went away; though his refined elegance was not lacking, there was no further news of him.
When Dulanshang took her leave, Zhang Shuo came back again and again, yet there was no further word from her. Is this not what is meant by that?

Prince Wenxuan was like the boat of Dai Kui, returning once his inspiration had ended—why must it be for the sake of lotuses? As the boat returned to the Pure Temple, he suddenly perceived a trail of fragrant dust.
Moving forward with the wind, I said: "How extraordinary! Could this be the young lady of the scattered sesame-rice who led me here to seek her out?
Or is it perhaps a deva from the Tuṣita Heaven descended to the mundane world? Indeed, I saw her by the edge of the lotus pond, with a jade-like face and rosy complexion.

In groups of three or two, they leaned languidly on their fragrant shoulders. Clad in green robes with yellow linings, their elegant garments adorned with floral hairpins, their countenances bloomed like lotuses and their forms revealed a radiant grace.
Far removed from the concerns of new acquaintances or old intimates, I encountered them amidst the lotus pools and the mulberry groves.
This is surely the lingering spirit from the "Stone of Three Lifetimes. There is no need to further lament this body; though its nature differs, it remains eternally present.
Behold its carefree transcendence of the mundane, its lofty purity and secluded tranquility. It dwells in spontaneous self-sufficiency, needing no pity from others.
It is like Lady Muren before she emerged from the thatched hut, or when the son of Ai was still a commoner, hidden at the Ligua Pass. Once the profound mechanism [of the Way] is realized—

She entered the inner chambers like Lady Guan Sunyan. Her long whistles echoed through the mountain gorges; she was as ethereal and poised as Zhang Lihua about to take flight, or Qin Nongyu ascending slowly upon her phoenix.
She was like the maiden who welcomed her lover at the mouth of the Tiantai Cavern, or the immortal who hosted a banquet within Mount Luofu.
A subtle fragrance occasionally wafted forth, as if she had ingested *jingjing* elixir; her feathered robes swirled in a dance.
Having once roamed the Cold Palace of the Moon, this single encounter was surely it. Yet she has entered the ranks of the Aqin maidens;
what need is there to speak of Jin or Wei, when she is unaware even of the Han? It is as if a celestial wind had blown her down, unwilling to permit the name Feiqiong to fall among mortals.
I laughed and said, "Was it not you, in the night of days past, at Fenglin Temple?"
"Is it that you have become weary and exhausted, and thus receive my teaching? You are indeed worthy of instruction. Now let us test our balance and debate.
When I was still under twenty years of age, we met by chance on the banks of the Xiling River.

Had you been able at that time to avoid the clamor and splendor, to transcend the mundane world, and to exert yourself in self-discipline, you would long since have been among the people of the heavens; even I might have been so as well."
He is to be admired from afar, yet cannot be approached intimately. Why have you encountered the *ming-yi* (the eclipse of light) and fallen into such distress?
It is because you have not yet tasted the bitterness of suffering and your resolve has not yet been firmened; this is simply your own indolence.

If, by the side of Fenglin Temple, you had lightly accepted my instruction yet remained immersed in the five turbidities, who knows what state you would be in today? How could one attain such transcendence as this?

"Xianxian! This, moreover, is your own realization. Suppose that all those in the world who are feverish with worldly passions and like dust-dust guests were to receive your teachings and then shake out their robes to walk away in lofty retirement—then why would it be necessary for me to prattle on with the Dharma and ascend the dais?

The *I Ching* speaks of 'the prosperous withdrawal' and 'the auspicious withdrawal,' praising the gentleman who encompasses all within his grasp. How much more so, then, regarding the Peach Blossom Spring..."
"Retreat and seclusion—this is the wisdom of the immortal at Tianmu. Since you have already become an immortal in embryo, I too have no intention of remaining in the world of men.
For now, I urge you to advance further, even to the top of a hundred-foot pole.
I have heard that ten trillion lands to the west of here, there is a pool of the seven treasures. Within it, there is neither old nor young, neither honor nor disgrace, and neither woman nor—"
O man, those who possess the resolute vow to be reborn [in the Pure Land] shall all realize the Great Enlightenment of the Golden Immortal (the Buddha).

Since your clan has produced many such individuals among its ranks, you are even more distinguished than your peers. You shall beat the cloud-lute and drink the jade nectar, chanting and pacing as an immortal who transcends the seven realms of existence and leaves behind the corpse-demons.
You must purify your heart and precede me in setting the whip; do not fail to live up to these three encounters.
Yet there are three things that are beneficial. Those beautiful women all rely on a gentle breeze to nod their heads and incline their hearts;
they are in perfect accord without a word. The many fragrances fold their robes in deference, and I too wish to sleep. If you, my two or three friends, wish to carry them away with you, I say:

"It must not be so. Fragrance and scent cause lofty aspirations to crumble; form and sound destroy one's physical vigor and lifespan. To distance oneself from them is easy for a man of integrity; to draw near to them is difficult."
[The interlocutor] said, "How is it that you alone disregard the reproach of the Lotus Spirit? Are you not being cautious?
Two or three of the disciples asked, "If so, why does the Master alone linger with such lingering affection? Does your mother also favor beauty? I replied, "It is not so.

My fondness for beauty is not like that of the common world; I simply admire her virtue. It is because I have encountered the lotuses of West Lake three times that I have undergone these three transformations."
His demeanor was like that of one who has undergone a single transformation; having reached the state of "the first transformation at Lu," his realization of the Way was pristine and untainted.
He was a man of great refinement and lofty purity who had transcended the mundane world; thus, I delighted in associating with him.

Now, the *Guanju* (Cuckoo of the River) expresses joy without excess, for it contemplates the *yaotiao* (lovely and remote) woman to be a match for the noble lord, lamenting the lack of worthy talent rather than indulging in carnal passion. Ruan Sizong (Ruan Ji) spent his days in close intimacy [with such men].
A neighboring girl, though not his wife, did not die with him; she went further to mourn him. Was this not one who truly cherished beauty yet was not licentious?
Therefore, I have used a metaphorical narrative and entrusted it to the image of a beautiful woman. As the poem says: "Upon whom does my thought dwell? On the beautiful woman in the west."

"May I perhaps encounter him morning or evening? This is also my own aspiration. For the sake of the Dharma-abbot of Yúan, Layman Yúyuán, who was sealing the reliquary chamber, I composed these words for the sealing of the lid and presented them to him, saying:
"Layman Yúyuán, you are one of the ancestral Buddhas and patriarchs from of old, practicing for yourself and transforming others."
This is the place where one establishes one's person and sustains one's life. Have you first established yourself here and dwelt in peace?

Having long possessed the power of aspiration and heard the Way, since you first took up residence in this monastery, you have been true in every matter. You have maintained your resolve in steadfast poverty, showing no regard for worldly conventions.
You have exhausted your mind and strength to uphold the ancestral path and the Dharma-gate; your integrity is steep and towering, such that it is difficult [to emulate].

He was straightforward and candid in his speech, appearing perhaps to disregard common human sentiment; yet he disregarded the slanders and jealousies of others, acting only according to what he deemed his duty.
His observance of the precepts was meticulous, and he clearly possessed the spirit of the patriarchs. Possessing vast learning and profound eloquence, he was truly eminent.
It would be impossible not to say that he did not disgrace our lineage, for it cannot be that he did not come here by virtue of his original vows.

As for the matters of his own practice and his work in transforming others, they were nearly completed; yet, suddenly withdrawing from this "place of heat," he anticipated his end by fasting until his passing.

His monastic quarters have been entrusted to capable successors—if one can achieve such things, that is sufficient. Why must one live for a hundred years or a thousand autumns? For the world often harbors a hatred for long life.

I do not consider it long; rather, I rejoice that you have early awakened to the True Constant. For that which has birth and extinction, coming and going, and length and shortness is the vision of worldly people.
That which is without length or shortness, without coming or going, and without extinction or birth is the solitary manifestation of the Original Reality.
Having awakened to the True Constant, then life is acceptable and death is acceptable, and going is also acceptable.

It may be so. To come is acceptable; to be tall is acceptable; to be short is also acceptable. However, the northern continent (Uttarakuru) is the breeding ground for the ignorant and the field for the profligate.

It is a place where one lives as a thief to attain long life in the heavens, yet it is one of the eight difficult conditions (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ). Like an old crane by the water who hears nothing, such a person, though long-lived, is actually premature in death.
Though existing, they are extinguished; though born, they die. The World-Honored One Sun-Face was born in the morning and perished by evening;
Ruci Tathāgata practiced as soon as he heard the Way. Thus, though brief, it is long; though departed, he remains; though dead, he lives.

If you understand this, you will be free from regret regarding the length or brevity of life and death. For now, I shall briefly cite a well-known *gong'an* to enable you to settle yourself and give rise to its function:
"The Buddha of Great Universal Wisdom sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him.
Yet, on the very day Maitreya World-Honored One left the household life, he immediately realized the Nirvana of the Three Virtues. This is not because his faculties were deficient.
There are those of sharp and dull faculties; the Path has its difficulties and its ease. Looking to his left and right, he said: "Tell me, after all, for what reason is this?
It is appropriate to respond with either prolixity or brevity, thereby indicating length or brevity. Sealed.
Preface to the Collection of Impromptu Verses Written While Dwelling in the Market: Chao Fu shook his head and refused to stay; the inhabitants all dwell together in the source of the Wuling River.

This is merely the reclusion of one who avoids the marketplace and the court. As for Dongfang Shuo, he sought seclusion at the Gate of the Golden Horse; Sima Jizhu set up his stall in the marketplace.
The marketplace of Chang’an is, from the outset, no different from the court; yet it does not forfeit its lofty character. Why is this?

For one who avoids both worldly sentiment and artificial refinement, even the marketplace and the court are like mountain caves. Why must one gaze longingly toward the distance and flee them before one may be considered lofty?
The spirit of Yinzhanzi was free and detached, and he certainly did not seek advancement at court; yet even so, he did not...

You once sought to distance yourself from the fluctuations of the marketplace and the bustling of the neighborhood shops, where one pursues a profit of ten or twenty percent; how lowly such pursuits are!
Yet, when you showed me your *Shijū màn yǒng jí* (Collected Wandering Verses on Dwelling in the Market), I was moved by its reflections on the times and its observations of things.

Its phrasing is concise yet far-reaching, and its meaning is pure and serene; it bears the lingering influence of Yuanliang (Tao Qian). Within its intervals, you reveal the worldly phenomena as being inseparable from the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The principle of non-separation is perhaps akin to that of one who enters a bustling marketplace to observe the transformations of the world while remaining inwardly tranquil.
Zhang Wenchang said, "The Master has already attained the Way; he dwells in peace even amidst the marketplace. You are surely such a person. Thus it is.

To look down with contempt upon one’s own body as being in the rivers and lakes while the heart remains at the imperial palace, or to have a form dwelling in mountains and forests while the consciousness dwells in the marketplace—how can such a person be considered either worthy or unworthy?
As for the "Great Recluse in the Market," I have seen it in the case of Yin-yanzi (the Son of the Drawn Rock); he was like Chao Fu and the Fisherman.
How could one not be left staring in their wake? As I read through this collection with a blunt mind, I was as bewildered as a fisherman who has mistakenly entered the Peach Blossom Spring;
I knew only of the peach blossoms and the roosters and dogs, for how could I have known the profound depth of that immortal realm?
"Equalizing Things":
Wei Ya's farmer wishes to equalize all things. A phoenix has embroidered plumage, yet lacks the timber for night-time construction;
a great elephant bears heavy loads, yet lacks the skill for galloping. Confucius and Mencius upheld benevolence and righteousness, yet lacked the means for hegemonic states.

It is due to karma. Thus, a common bird in a window compared to the phoenix, a mediocre horse compared to the great elephant, and Guan Zhong and Yan Ying compared to Confucius and Mencius—each excels in one capacity while failing in another;
the two [latter] are equally deficient in the other. Alas! How many deluded people there are in this world!

By nature, I am not skilled at calligraphy, nor do I desire to master it; for even if one’s writing were refined, it would merely constitute the talent of a minor clerk who transcribes documents. Yet, I have a passion for the calligraphy of the ancients.

However, being born of humble origins, I lament that I cannot read all the books of the ancients to peer through the gates of Confucius and Mencius. As for the Way of literature, I am even less capable.

Dreaming of a piebald horse is merely grasping at its fine hairs. Yet among the people of this world, some grant their approval based on a thorough knowledge of literary principles, while others grant it to me for my skill in calligraphy.
They say, "This person is skilled in writing but dull-witted; that person understands literature but is clumsy with the brush.

To claim that one is capable in one area and incapable in another—that these two individuals are exactly equal and no different—is a great delusion. Alas! How much such confusion prevails in the world!
What a deluded man you are! You claim that I am well-versed in literary principles; I truly dare not accept such a thing.

Yet, to place those who merely transcribe others' works on an equal footing with those who promote the nature and principle of the sages and worthies, as well as their writings—this is something I find particularly unbearable to hear.
It would be to cast Confucius, Mencius, Ban Gu, and Sima Qian into the same class as petty clerks who merely copy texts.
He regards Confucius, Mencius, Ban Gu, and Sima Qian as mere copyists and minor clerks.

Although his family elder’s moral character and literary talent have penetrated the innermost sanctuaries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he is unable to compose words for worldly dissemination to flatter the deaf and vulgar.
Yet the people of the world say: "Master Tianxi’s virtue and conduct are lofty, yet he lacks eloquence;

Master [So-and-so] is able to skillfully accommodate the ignorant laity, yet his grasp of the Dharma is deficient. One is capable and the other is not; thus the two masters are considered equal. How can such equality be anything but a distinction?

Is it like comparing a common bird to a phoenix, or comparing Guan Zhong and Yan Ying to Confucius and Mencius? By extending this reasoning, one sees that the world’s notion of equality is merely superficial.

As for "things," this refers to this entire category. From where could one investigate them to verify their reality? Thus we know that those who dwell as farmers in the wilds of Wei have been no fewer in ancient and modern times.
[This concludes] the "Equalizing Things" chapter.
It is indeed unfortunate that my talent and learning have not been mastered in the art of calligraphy. Yet, there is also a measure of fortune:
during the previous dynasty, the two masters Mr. Feng Jiqu and Mr. Lu Jingcheng were men of towering talent and eminent reputation, figures who transcend the ages.

While serving in the Inner Hanlin Academy, they were repeatedly suppressed by superficial critics because their clerical script was not considered refined enough; consequently, they were unable to join the ranks of the famous Shen and Gu.
It was not recorded. Thus we know that comparing talent and learning to the transcription of texts is like comparing physical features;
is this not a blessing within misfortune?

"In the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, being sincere and devoted even in this degenerate age; such individuals may be entrusted with great responsibility. Indeed, in these later generations, the observance of precepts and the practice of goodness have declined.

Yet, if there are those capable of personally cultivating these virtues without indolence, I know that they can certainly be relied upon as a great support. Looking back, the Way of Awakening stretches across all."

Throughout the universe, whether one is wise or foolish, noble or base, the sublime words [of the Buddha] proclaimed on Vulture Peak are equally applicable to all. Indeed, they are recorded as the instructions for every household and family.
How could one still remain fettered by the mere regulation of body and speech? Nor is it merely about exalting the practice of giving coins or pointing toward the granary.
Nevertheless, Upāli was preeminent in the Vinaya and was ranked foremost among the multitude of sages; the Kāñcanamālā Dhūta-dhara likewise manifested his excellence.
The banner of sharing the seat flourishes even more in a sagely age; how much more so in these final times! Yet, can one not anticipate the conditions of these final times?
What matter is there that cannot be known as clearly as looking at the palm of one's hand? Only that the golden coffin’s radiance has become hidden and the Sage has been gone for a long time;
while our practice is no longer in its full vigor, it is nevertheless still possible to act. It is said: "After five hundred years, liberation [is attained]; after another five hundred..."
In upholding the precepts, there was long-standing dedication; yet those of different dispositions were not many.

When the teaching of the Elephant (Buddhism) declined and the human heart no longer conformed to antiquity, it became vastly different from its former state. Nevertheless, that which can still be relied upon is this:

after five hundred years, one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); after another five hundred years, one cultivates merit. Although outward activities may be lax, patience and goodness can still be attained. Below this, however, [the fifth period] follows.

At a hundred years of age, one becomes increasingly frail and incapable. People engage in strife and contention, harboring hearts of cruelty and violence; they are predatory and greedy, regarding only profit as their goal.
At such a time, can there still be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit? It is our hope that we may encounter such persons at any moment.
Those who don the black robes and transcend the mundane world ought truly to maintain the Vinaya with strict purity; yet, in this degenerate age, this is not so.

The wisdom-mind has become base and thin, while the five desires are practiced openly. Licentious retribution and the proclamation of lewdness have caused the path of integrity and shame to be severed.
This state of debauchery and disorder has become a prevailing custom, such that even kings and ministers turn their eyes askance, and the Way of Awakening is treated with contempt.
Is this not a time when malevolent spirits, donning the robes of monks, steal away the True Dharma, and the Most Holy One weeps bitter tears of grief? It is precisely at such a time as this—

There was Jianmuxa, who, having been refined by the holy transformation, cast off worldly attachments and pursued the path. His evil habits had persisted for a long time, and he fanned the winds of heterodoxy.

Yet he was also uniquely capable of being uplifted and brought into the fold. Furthermore, those whose sentiments dwell upon transcending the world ought to rely on the provisions of a hundred blessings;
yet these common folk instead deepen their involvement with monasteries to fill their own purses and bags, slaughtering livestock and plowing fields to cultivate every kind of evil.

I report this: calculating by the hour and selling by the day, he trafficked like a peddler in the name of the Tathāgata. Consequently, he was born into the world to encounter the king’s law, thereby bringing disgrace upon the ranks of the Sangha.
This was surely a day when a heretic took an evil oath to destroy my teaching, and the Sugata’s radiance was eclipsed and shorn of its light.
Thus, he cultivated pure goodness; as one who assisted the noble traditions, he cast aside the floating clouds of power and profit to establish a beacon for the monastic community.
This too was a manifestation of an extraordinary birth. Alas for the blessings of the precepts! How they have been neglected in this sagely age.
Yet those who will appear in the future are rarely encountered. Thus it is said, "There are those who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit.
To say "there are" implies that such people are absent in the末法 (mofa, the final age); even when they do occasionally appear, they are as rare as one or two among hundreds of millions.
I contemplate the latter five hundred years and the difficulty of maintaining the precepts; their conduct lacks excess, yet they are but teachers for insects among bhikṣus.
It is being eroded from within; inevitably, there will be collective attacks and mutual disparagement, which is truly lamentable.

To wish to revive the collapsing order at such a time is like exposing a single plant to the sun while ten others remain in the cold—it is difficult to say how this could ever succeed. Reflect again on the difficulty of cultivating merit during the final five hundred years.

While virtuous deeds require only diligence, laypeople are steeped in bias and corrupt influences, and even among the monastics, there are those who possess not so much as a thread or half a grain of integrity.
"Beans! How difficult this is! At that time, I wished to practice my Way, yet I was surrounded by those of Qi while being swarmed by the multitude of Chu—is this not indeed difficult?
Nevertheless, were it not for this difficulty, there would be no way to manifest one who is a peerless and extraordinary talent.
Now, as for those who delight in [the Dharma], it is something all human beings naturally love; yet they are able to maintain the precepts. As for those who lend their wealth...

He is one toward whom all under heaven turn in common, yet he has been able to cultivate merit. I know that his endowment from past lives was extraordinary, such that the life of wisdom may be entrusted to him;
this too is what I have observed and known as my own days draw to a close.

Regarding the two phrases concerning the "final five hundred years," there are pressing matters in these degenerate times. It is simply that both the ordained and the laity must each fulfill their respective paths.

Thus, while *bhikṣus* should master the Vinaya scriptures and those of pure conduct should revere the "Three Multitudes" (the Three Jewels), such things are difficult to achieve in the Dharma-ending age; yet, they do indeed exist. This is certainly not... [omitted].
This is indeed a matter for the common man. In the past, the Great Sage surveyed all directions from his lofty vantage point and looked down upon future generations;

who, then, would be those capable of bearing the burden of the life of wisdom? It is said: they must be those who, during the final five hundred years, are able to uphold the precepts and cultivate merit.

Among the monastic community (*śramaṇa*), the assembly shall be vast and the study of the *Prātimokṣa* (the code of discipline) shall be refined; among the lay followers (*upāsaka*), the ranks shall be numerous and they shall delight in making offerings without weariness. Thus, through mutual support and cooperation, they shall bring it to fruition.
It is accomplished. I know that even in times of decline, one may still be uplifted, for the Buddha’s wisdom remains unobstructed. Why is this?
When the True Man responds to the destiny of the age, the dragons and elephants raise up the profound light of the primary truth (*paramārtha*). This need not be discussed;

yet even in the final five hundred years, when malevolent spirits abound and depravity flows rampant, those who preside over the Dharma-gate treat children, jade, and silks as their concern, while those called "monks" shout out for slaughter.

Lu! It is because of such individuals that their perverse winds prevail. Those who can go against the current of the masses, personally upholding the precepts and disciplinary codes to instruct those who come to study, and thereby stem the surging tide of madness—these must be bhikṣus.
They are truly the disciples of the Sage and the very foundation upon which the life of wisdom relies.
When I reflect on this, the entrustment of the robes and bowl to the dhūta practitioners likely refers to this. Moreover, as for the sphere of the sacred teachings...
Xuán. The management of the Bamboo Grove and the Jeta Grove was once indeed flourishing. Yet, as we approach the final five hundred years [of the Dharma], my Way gradually declines.
Who can distinguish between the waters of the Shéng and the Zī? Those who hasten toward power and profit see only the profusion of the five desires;

those who maintain their integrity and pure conduct rarely receive offerings of *kaṣāya* (vegetarian food). Thus, they become solely those who assist in the construction of sin. If there are those capable of contributing from their purses and bags...
Those who plant the banner of the *caitya* and distance themselves from heterodox teachers in order to support the establishment of the True Dharma must be laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
These are surely those with whom the Sages have entrusted the task, and who are capable of upholding the Buddha’s wisdom. I have reflected on this twice:

the Buddha’s teachings were entrusted to kings and ministers; is it not for this reason? Some may say they are among the multitude who hear the Dharma, yet the path is vast—how could it be limited to only these two?
Is this sufficient? I reply: Although the number of the virtuous and wise is great, they do not lie outside the ranks of the ordained and the laity;

yet in these degenerate times, the essential priority for propagating and extending the Dharma must be the precepts and merit. Nevertheless, how could the Sage not desire that all people in the world maintain the precepts and cultivate merit?

It is simply because we encounter a declining age that circumstances prevent us from accomplishing both simultaneously. Therefore, if one can truly exert oneself to the utmost in each, [the goal will be achieved].
